body.p: Claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 are pending in the application.
The Examiner rejects claim 9 under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
The applicants respectfully traverse this rejection.
The Examiner asserts:
"Re. Claim 9: Although "a force applied to a skin of the user" has been defined,
such a force is used to define the function of the force transducer with relation to
a general force, and not the force of the PPG sensor against the skin.
"To further clarify the rejection: claim 9 states that a force transducer

measures a general forceapplied to the skin of the user. There is no element which applies a specific force having antecedent basis, nor recitation of a certain force applied to the user - only the recitation of a device which is capable of measuring such force." (Office action, page 3, lines 8-14,
emphasis added.)

The applicants respectfully disagree with this assertion. The preamble to claim 9 indicates that a force transducer can measure a force applied to the skin. The applicants concur that this could refer to a "general force".
However, contrary to the Examiner's assertion that claim 9 does not recite "the force of the PPG sensor against the skin", claim 9 specifically recites:
"measuring, by the force transducer, a measured force at which the contact
surface of the PPG sensor is pressed against a skin of a user" (Claim 9, lines 13- 14, emphasis added).
Subsequent references to this force specifically refer to "the measured force", and not the general "force" referred to by the Examiner.
In the interest of advancing prosecution in this case, the preamble to claim 9 is amended herein to eliminate the reference to the "force transducer that measures a force applied to the skin".
Withdrawal of this rejection is respectfully requested.
The Examiner rejects claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada et al. (USPA 2007/0055163, hereinafter Asada) and Nitzan (USPA 2018/0325398).
The applicants respectfully traverse this rejection.
1. Asada does not disclose analyzing a pulsative AC component of a PPG waveform.
The Examiner asserts:
"Although Asada describes the use of analyzing a pulsatile AC

component of a plethysmographicwaveform, Asada does not explicitly state that the output of the plethysmographic sensor of their invention comprises a DC component and an AC component" (Office action, page 4, lines 15-17,
emphasis added).
This assertion is clearly erroneous.
The Examiner does not identify where Asada provides this disclosure, and in the Office action of 12 May 2021, the Examiner specifically states:
"Asada does not explicitly teach the invention wherein information is
extracted regarding a blood volume pulse from an AC component of an output signal of the PPG sensor" (Office action of 12 May 2021, page 5, fourth
paragraph, emphasis added.)
Because the Examiner fails to identify where Asada discloses analyzing a

pulsative AC component, the applicants respectfully maintain that the Examiner has failed to establish a prima facie case to support the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14- 21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada and Nitzan, and respectfully maintain that this rejection should be withdrawn.
2. The combination of Asada and Nitzan does not disclose mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information to a blood pressure value.
The Examiner asserts that Nitzan provides this teaching.

"[Nitzan teaches] ... when the measured force reaches a predetermined force value, map the extracted information to a blood pressure value at the measured force applied to the skin of the user via the contact surface ofthe PPG sensor (Paragraph 0057, Figs. 1A, 1 B: gradual decreases in cuff pressure and mapping of certain points of cuff pressure to mean, systolic, and diastolic blood pressures...)" (Office action, page 5, last paragraph, lines 1- 4, emphasis added.)
The Examiner's assertion that Nitzan discloses mapping the blood volume information to a blood pressure value is clearly erroneous.

As acknowledged by the Examiner, Nitzan discloses mapping the cuff pressure to blood pressure values. Nitzan does not disclose mapping the blood volume pulse information to blood pressure values, as specifically taught and claimed by the applicants.

Because the Examiner fails to identify where the combination of Asada and Nitzan discloses mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information to a blood pressure value, and because the Examiner acknowledges that Nitzan discloses mapping the cuff pressure to blood pressure values, the applicants respectfully maintain that the Examiner has failed to establish a prima facie case to support the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada and Nitzan, and respectfully maintain that this rejection should be withdrawn.
3. The combination of Asada and Nitzan does not disclose mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information to a blood pressure value when the measured force reaches a predetermined force value.
To utilize the mapping between the AC component and the mean arterial
pressure illustrated in FIG. 4, a force of approximately 17.25N must be applied; at force levels that are substantially different than 17.25N, the mapping of FIG. 4 will not be valid.

Neither Asada nor Nitzan, individually or collectively, teach or suggest applying a particular pressure (e.g. 17.25N), and mapping the AC component of the PPG signal at that particular force level to a blood pressure value (e.g. FIG. 4).
The Examiner asserts:

"Examiner notes that gradual increasing/decreasing in pressure and identification of fiducial points during the gradual pressure changes reads upon a "predetermined force value," since the values of a ramp function are predetermined within a range; Examiner further notes that limiting an applied pressure or range of pressures based on another detected signal component also reads upon a "predetermined" pressure since the criteria for limiting the pressure is predetermined" (Office action, page 5, last paragraph, continuing
to page 6).
The applicants respectfully disagree that a range of force values can reasonably be interpreted as "a predetermined force value".
However, even assuming in argument that a range of force values can

reasonably be interpreted as a predetermined force value, the applicants note that the Examiner's assertion does not address the claimed element of mapping the AC component of the PPG signal to a blood pressure value when a particular force is applied.
As is common in the art, and as the Examiner's assertion implies, the cuff

pressure is gradually decreased until a particular PPG event occurs, and the pressure at which the event occurs is mapped to a blood pressure value. That is, in Asada and Nitzan, the PPG signal is used as a 'trigger' to cause the recording of the measured force (cuff pressure) when the trigger occurs. The operation of the applicants' claimed invention is completely opposite. In the applicants' claimed invention, the measured force is used as a 'trigger' to cause the recording of the PPG signal when the trigger occurs.
Because the combination of Asada and Nitzan does not teach or suggest

mapping the extracted blood volume pulse information to a blood pressure value when the measured force reaches a predetermined force value, the applicants respectfully maintain that the Examiner has failed to establish a prima facie case to support the rejection of claims 1-2, 5-10, 12, 14-21, and 23-25 under 35 U.S.C. 103 over Asada and Nitzan, and respectfully maintain that this rejection should be withdrawn.

In view of the foregoing, the applicants respectfully request that the Examiner withdraw the rejections of record, allow all the pending claims, and find the application to be in condition for allowance.
